summary: This informational document describes ways to support multicast listeners in Proxy Mobile IPv6 domains without changing the mobility or multicast standards. The Local Mobility Anchor acts as the multicast anchor, and Mobile Access Gateways handle listener signaling. It shows how to deploy existing parts together.

plainLanguage.summary: When your phone moves between network access points, you still want shared broadcasts like TV. This explains how to arrange existing pieces so that keeps working.

questions: how do mobile nodes receive multicast in pmipv6
subtitle: How to support multicast listeners when mobile nodes move between access points.

tldr.problem: Proxy Mobile IPv6 manages mobility transparently on the network side without requiring mobile nodes to participate, but multicast (one-way group communication like TV broadcasts) needs special handling when nodes move between access points.
tldr.mechanism: The Local Mobility Anchor (LMA) acts as a multicast anchor point, and Mobile Access Gateways implement MLD proxy functions to intercept and forward multicast subscriptions and data, tunneling them through the mobility infrastructure.
tldr.outcome: Mobile nodes can subscribe to and receive multicast without any changes to the mobility or multicast standards; multicast works transparently across handovers.

facts.label: Query behavior on handover
facts.value: MAG sends General Query immediately after address config

facts.label: Scope of sender support
facts.value: Listeners only; sender mobility is out of scope

facts.label: IPv4 and IPv6 support
facts.value: Both via IGMP and MLD proxies

today: RFC 6224 is Informational and describes a practical approach to multicast in PMIPv6 domains. It is not obsoleted and remains relevant for deployments that combine network-based mobility (PMIPv6) with multicast services.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) is a network-based mobility protocol that manages IP address continuity for mobile nodes without requiring them to run mobility protocols. When a mobile node moves between network access points (called Mobile Access Gateways), the network infrastructure (specifically the Local Mobility Anchor and the MAGs) handles all the mobility signaling automatically.

However, PMIPv6 does not directly address multicast communication, which is one-way group transmission (like television or push notifications). Multicast relies on group membership signaling protocols like MLD (Multicast Listener Discovery for IPv6) or IGMP (for IPv4). In standard Mobile IPv6, bidirectional tunneling to a home agent could be used for multicast, but in PMIPv6, a node is unaware of mobility and does not initiate such tunneling after a handover.

RFC 6224 describes how to deploy multicast in PMIPv6 domains without modifying any mobility or multicast standards. The solution uses MLD/IGMP proxy functions at the MAGs and designates the LMA as the multicast anchor point.
sections.plainLanguage: Proxy Mobile IPv6 usually handles moving between access points invisibly, but multicasts (broadcasts) need special care. This document explains how to set up the network so broadcasts follow you as you move.

sections.title: Network Architecture and Concepts
sections.content:
In the PMIPv6 multicast deployment, three entities work together. The Local Mobility Anchor (LMA) is a router that acts as a multicast subscription anchor point (similar to a home agent in Mobile IPv6). The Mobile Access Gateway (MAG) is an access router that handles nodes at a given access point and implements MLD proxy functions. Each MAG maintains one MLD proxy instance per unique LMA it serves; an MLD proxy allows multiple downstream nodes to share upstream group membership by aggregating their subscriptions.

A mobile node is transparent to all of this: it joins and leaves multicast groups using standard MLD Report and Leave messages on its local link, just as if it were in the fixed Internet. The mobile node is unaware of the mobility domain and uses its link-local address for MLD signaling.

When an MN joins a group, it sends an MLD Report on its access link. The MAG (acting as an MLD proxy) intercepts this, updates its proxy membership database, and sends an aggregated Join to the LMA over the unicast tunnel that connects them. Multicast data from the Internet arrives at the LMA, which forwards it according to its multicast routing state. The LMA sends the data down the tunnel to the MAG, and the MAG forwards it to the MN's access link.
sections.plainLanguage: The LMA is like a television broadcast station. Each MAG is like a cable relay that intercepts requests from viewers and forwards them to the station, then sends the broadcast signals down to the viewers.

sections.title: Handover and State Management
sections.content:
When a mobile node moves to a new MAG, the MAG first detects the arrival via a router solicitation message. PMIPv6 binding is established with the LMA for the node's unicast address. Then, to discover what multicast groups the MN wants to receive, the MAG sends an MLD General Query on the new access link (this is standard MLD querier behavior). The MN responds with MLD Reports indicating its group memberships.

The MAG then adds the new access link as a downstream interface to the appropriate MLD proxy instance (the one whose upstream tunnel goes to the corresponding LMA). If the MN's multicast subscriptions are new, the MAG sends updated MLD Reports to the LMA; if the LMA's proxy instance already has forwarding states for those groups, no new upstream message may be needed (to avoid unnecessary signaling).

During handover, the LMA does not need to send a General Query on the tunnel interface to refresh forwarding states; instead, the MAG triggers state updates by sending Reports that aggregate all its nodes' subscriptions. If the MAG loses an interface (the access link goes down), it updates the proxy membership database and may send an MLD Done (leave) message upstream if no other MN is subscribed to that group.
sections.plainLanguage: When a phone arrives at a new access point, the access point asks 'What broadcasts do you want to watch?' The phone answers, and the access point tells the central station which broadcasts to send down the tunnel.

sections.title: IPv4 Support, Multihoming, and Tuning
sections.content:
RFC 6224 also covers multicast for mobile nodes running IPv4 in a PMIPv6 domain. When IPv4 address mobility is enabled (via RFC 5844), mobile nodes use IGMP instead of MLD, and the MAGs provide IGMP proxy functions in the same manner as MLD proxies.

In multihoming scenarios (where an MN is attached to multiple MAGs or has multiple addresses), the architecture ensures that each MN receives traffic on the appropriate tree. Because MNs attached to different LMAs can subscribe to the same multicast group while connected to the same MAG, the network might carry redundant traffic, but the MN itself will not receive duplicate packets on a single interface.

For reliable operation, MLD timers and the Robustness Variable (defined in RFC 3810) should be carefully chosen to account for the time scales of handover operations and proxy configuration in the PMIPv6 domain. If an MLD Query is lost due to handover timing, the node might not respond, so timer values must be conservative.
sections.plainLanguage: This approach works with both IPv6 and IPv4. On faster or slower networks, the system might need tuning so that queries don't time out during phone handovers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 6224 notes that multicast source authentication (proving who is sending a given multicast stream) is outside the scope of the document. The focus is on listener subscription and data delivery.

Standard PMIPv6 and multicast security mechanisms remain applicable. The tunnels between MAGs and LMAs are part of the PMIPv6 infrastructure and should be protected by standard network security practices. Because multicast data flows through these tunnels, any cryptographic protection or rate limiting required for the domain should be enforced at the tunnel endpoints or at the MAG/LMA interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: This document assumes the network is already secure and does not describe how to prevent false broadcasters or attacks.
